nameStory: The Common House Spider earned its straightforward name by being the spider you're most likely to encounter in your home. Unlike many spiders that prefer the great outdoors, this species has become so closely associated with human dwellings that it's found worldwide wherever people live. It's truly made itself at home with us!
description: The Common House Spider is a small, brownish spider that builds the messy cobwebs you often find in corners of basements, garages, and under eaves. These spiders have rounded abdomens and relatively long, thin legs that they use to quickly navigate their tangled webs. They're typically about the size of a small button, with females being larger than males. Their webs look disorganized compared to the neat orb webs of garden spiders, but they're highly effective traps for flying insects.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds irregular, messy-looking cobwebs in corners and crevices that feel sticky and collect dust, creating those classic 'haunted house' webs

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Round, bulbous abdomen that looks like a small bead, often with a slightly mottled or chevron pattern visible on closer inspection

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Hangs upside down in web center or retreats to a corner when disturbed, vibrating the web rapidly when threatened

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body about the size of a pea (females) or smaller (males), with legs that would span roughly the diameter of a nickel

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Variable brownish coloration with darker chevron or herringbone patterns on the abdomen, often faded or indistinct

habitat: Found throughout New England in and around human structures, particularly in undisturbed corners of basements, garages, sheds, and under roof eaves. They prefer areas with some moisture and steady temperatures, often near windows where flying insects are attracted to lights. You'll also find them in woodpiles, rock walls, and other sheltered outdoor spaces close to buildings.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as temperatures warm, with mating occurring and egg sacs appearing in web corners. Webs may look fresher and more organized as spiders rebuild after winter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with the most visible adults hunting in webs. Multiple generations may overlap, and egg sacs are commonly found.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active but may become less visible as they prepare for winter. Late-season egg sacs are laid that will overwinter.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, but some may survive in heated buildings. Egg sacs remain dormant in protected areas until spring warming.

funFact: Common House Spiders are such frequent stowaways that they've accidentally colonized every continent except Antarctica by hitchhiking in human cargo - making them one of the most widely distributed spider species on Earth despite being only about the size of a pea!
confusionNotes: Often confused with cellar spiders (daddy longlegs spiders), but cellar spiders have much longer, thinner legs and build sheet-like webs rather than messy cobwebs. Remember: if the web looks like a miniature hammock, it's probably a cellar spider; if it looks like it needs housekeeping, it's likely a house spider.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'American House Spider' in some regions, this species is actually found worldwide and likely originated elsewhere before spreading with human commerce. The cobwebs they create are often what people think of as 'classic' spider webs in horror movies, though they're actually quite different from the beautiful orb webs most people picture when they think of spider webs.
compareHints: The closely related Wandering House Cobweaver has similar web-building habits but tends to move its web location more frequently and has slightly different abdominal markings. Common House Spiders are more likely to maintain the same web location for extended periods, constantly adding to and repairing their cobweb rather than relocating. Both species prefer indoor environments, but Common House Spiders are generally more sedentary once they establish a good hunting spot.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Common House Spider, the Wandering House Cobweaver is slightly smaller and much more likely to abandon its web site.
